The Middle East crisis and upended crude and fuel flows have accelerated a shift in the global tanker fleet that began last year.

A growing number of the so-called long-range-2 (LR2) clean tankers that have transported fuels such as diesel and gasoline have become the so-called dirty tankers and started shipping crude.

As of this week, a record-high share of 75% of the global LR2 fleet is engaged in dirty crude transportation, while the number and share of tankers moving petroleum products, the so-called clean vessels, have dropped to record lows, per Signal Ocean data compiled by Bloomberg.

The LR2 tankers are similar in capacity to the Aframax crude tankers, which can ship up to 800,000 barrels of crude each. With lower refinery output and fuel flows from the Middle East, due to damaged refineries and Hormuz disruptions, demand for clean tankers in the region has been lower, but demand for dirty vessels for crude transportation has spiked.

A clean-turned-dirty LR2 tanker could be employed on the complex trade shuffles near the Strait of Hormuz, where shuttle-shipments have become the prevailing mode of moving crude oil out of the Persian Gulf in recent months.

To be sure, the shift from clean to dirty tankers began in 2025, because of rising crude oil supply and longer voyages, and the need to store crude on water.

This year the clean-to-dirty changeover has accelerated because of more tankers needed to evacuate crude out of the Strait of Hormuz, and because of high crude freight rates that earn additional millions of dollars for ship owners and operators.

“The LR2 market has undergone a marked change in vessel employment since the start of 2025. Signal Ocean data show that dirty employment accounted for 74.2% of the LR2 fleet on 30 October 2026, compared with 53.0% on 1 January 2025,” Signal Ocean’s senior market analyst Maria Bertzeletou and freight analyst Georgios Sakellariou wrote in an analysis earlier this month.

“Whether this pattern persists will depend on relative earnings, cargo demand and the commercial incentives for vessels to return to clean service,” they said.
